lines: ARCHIVE DIVISION — THE SEALED FILE CO.

leads.title: The Case Closure
leads.question: Why was Naomi Vale's case closed after eleven days?
leads.detectiveNote: First thing that jumps out — eleven days. That's not an investigation, that's a formality. Someone closed this fast. I need to figure out why before I go any further.

unlockTask.prompt: What is the strongest issue with the original investigation?

options.text: The case was closed before a primary suspect was identified or ruled out
The missing person report was never properly filed with county records
The sheriff personally knew Naomi Vale and had a conflict of interest
The investigation ran for the standard minimum period before suspension

hints: Read the closure memo carefully. What is missing from it that you would expect to see in a proper investigation closure?
A real closure should document what was ruled out. This one doesn't. It closes without naming a suspect, without explaining the timeline gap, and without accounting for Naomi's complaint.
The answer is in what the memo does NOT include. No suspect named. No explanation for the 1 hour 42 minute gap. No mention of the internal complaint Naomi filed days before she disappeared.

onComplete.finding: The case was closed before the investigation was complete — no suspect named, no timeline explained, no complaint on record.

leads.title: The Timeline Gap
leads.question: Where was Naomi between leaving WHLW and the 911 call?
leads.detectiveNote: Two timestamps. One from a witness, one from emergency dispatch. They don't match. That gap in the middle — nearly two hours — is where the whole case lives.

unlockTask.prompt: What does the timeline gap most strongly suggest?

options.text: Naomi went somewhere between leaving the station and the 911 call — the gap is intentional and unaccounted for
The witness was mistaken about the time and the gap doesn't actually exist
The 911 call was delayed due to poor radio signal in the area
Naomi drove to a nearby town and the travel time explains the gap

hints: Compare the witness statement time to the 911 call timestamp. Calculate exactly how long the gap is — then ask yourself whether the map explains it.
The map shows Naomi's vehicle was recovered near the relay tower on Route 7. The station is close. The gap is too long to be explained by driving time alone.
The gap is 1 hour and 42 minutes. The drive from the station to the tower takes under 15 minutes. Something happened during those remaining 87 minutes that no one has accounted for.

onComplete.finding: There is an unexplained 1 hour 42 minute gap in Naomi's movements — far too long to be explained by travel time alone.

leads.title: Station Irregularities
leads.question: What was happening at WHLW before Naomi disappeared?
leads.detectiveNote: The broadcast schedule has a segment that shouldn't be there. The maintenance memo dances around something without saying it directly. Someone was doing something at that station that wasn't on any official record.

unlockTask.prompt: Which two pieces of evidence together most strongly suggest unauthorized activity at WHLW?

options.text: Broadcast Schedule — unauthorized midnight segment with initials E.V.
Maintenance Memo — after-hours archive access via consulting badge
Missing Person Report — Naomi's disappearance record
Staff Directory — only external consultants section carries those initials
Area Map — vehicle recovery location near the relay tower

hints: Look for evidence that documents something happening at the station itself — something that wasn't authorized or wasn't on any official log.
One document shows an unauthorized broadcast segment. Another shows unauthorized after-hours access to the station archive. Together they tell the same story.

The broadcast schedule shows a midnight segment authorized by initials E.V. — not in the standard rotation. The maintenance memo documents after-hours archive access using a consulting badge. Both point to the same person operating outside their sanctioned role.

onComplete.finding: Naomi was investigating unauthorized station activity — an unlisted broadcast segment and after-hours archive access, both connected to the same external party.

leads.title: The Caller
leads.question: Who or what was warning Naomi?
leads.detectiveNote: The same number, calling in week after week during Naomi's shift. Each call longer than the last. Someone was reaching out to her specifically. Whether that was a warning, a threat, or something else — I don't know yet.

unlockTask.prompt: What do the calls most likely represent?

options.text: Someone aware of the broadcast manipulation was trying to reach Naomi specifically
A regular listener who called in frequently during her show
A prank caller who happened to call during her shift
Station management checking in on the overnight broadcast

hints: Look at the pattern in the phone records — the same number, escalating frequency, always during Naomi's specific shift. That's not random.
Listen to the Caller 03 recording. The caller references something specific about 'what's on the air.' They know something about the broadcast content.

The calls escalate over the final weeks before Naomi's disappearance. The caller references the signal and seems to be warning her. This isn't a regular listener — this is someone who knew what was happening.

onComplete.finding: The calls suggest someone knew the WHLW broadcasts were being manipulated and was trying to warn Naomi.

leads.title: The Missing Tape
leads.question: Why does the cassette matter — and how did it get back to the station?
leads.detectiveNote: The tape shows up in the station archive after Naomi is already gone. That's the thing nobody explained. She couldn't have returned it. So who did?

unlockTask.prompt: Why was the cassette tape returned to the station archive after Naomi's disappearance?

options.text: Someone returned it deliberately — the experiment wasn't finished and an unlisted tape left out would draw attention
Naomi returned it herself before she disappeared
It was never removed — the personal effects inventory is inaccurate
A station employee found it in Naomi's belongings and returned it without knowing its significance

hints: Check the personal effects inventory. The tape is listed as recovered from the station archive — but Naomi was already gone when it was found there. Work backwards from that.
The tape was unlisted. An unlisted tape sitting in an archive would be noticed eventually. Whoever was using it needed it back in the system before anyone started asking questions.

The tape was returned by whoever ran the experiment. Leaving an unlisted tape in the archive was a loose end. Returning it quietly buried it alongside the legitimate inventory — and the experiment could continue.

onComplete.finding: The tape was returned to the station archive after Naomi's disappearance by whoever conducted the experiment — not by Naomi.

leads.title: Lena Hart's Trail
leads.question: What did Lena discover — and why did she disappear?
leads.detectiveNote: Naomi's younger sister. Twelve years old when Naomi disappeared. By 2006 she was a journalism student pulling on the same threads. She found something specific enough to get her killed. I need to find out what that was.

unlockTask.prompt: Which evidence most clearly shows that Lena identified a specific person connected to Naomi's disappearance?

options.text: Lena's blog archive — research notes on WHLW broadcast patterns
College photo — handwritten note on the reverse
Forum threads — Lena posted under her real name
Missing person report — original 1998 record

hints: Lena left something behind that points to a specific person — not just the station, not just the tapes, but a name. Look at every piece of evidence she produced.
The college photo has a note written on the back. Read it carefully. Lena wasn't just documenting the case — she was naming someone.
The note on the back of the college photo is Lena's most direct statement. She names the experiment and connects it to a specific individual at WHLW. That name is what got her killed.

onComplete.finding: Lena connected Naomi's evidence to a specific person at WHLW — and disappeared in March 2007 before she could publish her findings.

leads.title: Gabriel's Posts
leads.question: Who kept the case alive online — and what do they know?
leads.detectiveNote: Someone has been posting in Moth Hollow forums for years under an anonymous handle. They know too much to be a random true crime follower. The interview record from 1998 might tell me who this actually is.

unlockTask.prompt: Which two pieces of evidence together confirm the identity of the anonymous forum poster?

options.text: Forum threads — anonymous username active in Moth Hollow discussions
Missing person report — Gabriel Hart listed as interviewed family contact
Lena's blog archive — references to research collaboration
College photo — Lena's handwritten note

hints: The forum poster uses an anonymous handle but makes references that only someone close to the case would know. Cross-reference with the police interview record from 1998.
The missing person report lists family contacts interviewed. One of those names matches details the anonymous poster mentions in the forums that were never made public.

Gabriel Hart was interviewed in October 1998. The forum poster references details about Naomi's shift pattern and the family's private timeline — information that was never in any public record. It's Gabriel.

onComplete.finding: Gabriel Hart — Naomi and Lena's brother — has been the anonymous forum poster, searching for answers for over two decades.

leads.title: Dr. Elias Voss
leads.question: Who was Voss — and what was he doing at WHLW?
leads.detectiveNote: The initials on the broadcast schedule. The consulting badge in the maintenance memo. Lena named him. Now I need to understand exactly what he was running inside that station.

unlockTask.prompt: What was Dr. Voss conducting at WHLW?

options.text: An unauthorized behavioral conditioning experiment using the overnight broadcast signal
A licensed community psychology outreach program approved by station management
A frequency calibration study commissioned by the station's engineering team
A personal research project on radio audience demographics with no harmful intent

hints: Read Voss's academic paper alongside the calibration sheet. His published research describes exactly the methodology that the WHLW equipment was modified to support.
The therapy notes are redacted — but the visible sections describe patient responses that match the patterns Lena documented in her blog. The patients were WHLW listeners.

Voss's 1991 paper describes embedding behavioral response triggers in audio signals. The calibration sheet shows WHLW equipment was modified to exactly those specifications. The therapy notes document the effects on listeners. This was a live experiment on an unwitting public.

onComplete.finding: Voss used WHLW's overnight broadcast to run an unauthorized behavioral conditioning experiment on the station's listening audience.

leads.title: Naomi Knew
leads.question: Why did Naomi become a threat to Voss?
leads.detectiveNote: She filed a complaint five days before she disappeared. She named Voss. She had the tape. She had connected everything. For someone running an illegal experiment, Naomi was no longer just a problem — she was a deadline.

unlockTask.prompt: What made Naomi a direct threat to Voss specifically?

options.text: She discovered physical evidence of the experiment and filed a formal complaint naming Voss before she disappeared
She confronted Voss publicly at the station and threatened to go to the press
She had recorded Voss accessing the archive after hours and kept the footage
She had told multiple coworkers about her suspicions and word had reached Voss

hints: Look at the date on the internal complaint and the date of Naomi's disappearance. Then look at what the complaint actually says.
The complaint is dated October 9, 1998 — five days before Naomi disappeared. It names Voss directly and references the unauthorized broadcast segment.

Naomi filed a formal written complaint naming Voss, citing the unlisted tape and the unauthorized segment. That complaint — if it had entered the official record — would have ended the experiment and exposed Voss. It never made it into the case file.

onComplete.finding: Naomi filed a formal complaint naming Voss five days before she disappeared. The complaint was never entered into the official investigation record.

leads.title: The Tower
leads.question: What happened on the night of October 14, 1998?
leads.detectiveNote: Everything points to the relay tower on Route 7. Naomi's car. The search photos. The restricted incident report. One more thing — there's an authorization code somewhere in this archive. Find it.

fields.label: Authorization code to access restricted file EV-014
fields.hint: The code appears somewhere in the evidence archive. Look at documents that reference case numbers or file IDs.

fields.label: Who confronted Naomi at the relay tower?
fields.hint: Only one person had both the motive and the knowledge of where Naomi would be that night.

fields.label: Why did Voss go to the tower?

options.text: To silence Naomi before her complaint could be investigated
To retrieve the cassette tape she had taken from the archive
To warn Naomi that her life was in danger from a third party
To offer Naomi compensation in exchange for her silence

hints: You need three things: the authorization code, a suspect, and a motive. The code is in the archive. The suspect is already revealed. The motive follows directly from the complaint.
The authorization code MH-7734 appears in the case documentation. The suspect is Dr. Voss. The motive: the complaint she filed would have exposed and ended everything he had spent years building.
Voss followed Naomi to the tower — the only place she would be alone that night, far from the station, after the shift. The complaint made her a deadline. The tower made it possible.

onComplete.finding: Naomi confronted Voss at the relay tower on October 14, 1998. Voss silenced her before her complaint could be investigated. The case was closed eleven days later with no charges filed.

solution.revealStory: Dr. Elias Voss spent four years conducting an unauthorized behavioral conditioning experiment through WHLW's overnight broadcast signal. When Naomi Vale discovered the unlisted tapes and filed a formal complaint naming him, she gave him a deadline. On the night of October 14, 1998, Voss followed her to the relay tower on Route 7 — the one place she would be alone and unreachable. The case was closed eleven days later by a sheriff's department that never received her complaint. Lena Hart found the same trail eight years later. She disappeared in March 2007. The experiment is over. The evidence is here. The case is yours to close.
